# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Gets Upstairs

If you've ever stood in a shower on the fortieth floor of a skyscraper and wondered why the water comes out with satisfying force, you've witnessed a quiet triumph of engineering. The water in that pipe may have traveled dozens of miles, been pushed uphill hundreds of feet, and passed through a choreographed system of pumps, tanks, and pressure valves before arriving at your showerhead. Let's trace that journey, using a concrete example that we'll follow from beginning to end.

## The Fundamental Physics: Elevation Is Everything

Water pressure in a municipal system is fundamentally about gravity. Every foot of elevation between a water source and your tap generates roughly 0.43 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure. This means that a reservoir sitting on a hill 200 feet above your neighborhood provides about 86 psi of pressure at ground level—before a single pump is involved.

This is why cities historically built reservoirs on the highest available ground. New York's Catskill aqueducts deliver water from reservoirs in the mountains, and gravity alone carries it nearly a hundred miles to the city. The engineers who designed these systems in the early twentieth century were essentially harvesting elevation.
